title: Can GROUP BY still be optimized after all these years?

toddbandrowsky · Nov 7, 2026

You know, I have a hard time seeing how it can be cheaper to run a dataset across a wire rather than just send its grouped results. That's really the problem. I mean, who cares if it takes 100ns to group by on a box when it will take 10 times much for the data to get to it and back.

The fastest possible group by is in sequential memory on that box, fetched from an nvme.

So, when we do group by partitioning, we're really saying, put the groups themselves on different boxes, and group the group by. If it were some utter megaset, the place to put it is on a mainframe, which is basically created for purposes of group by on ridiculous datasets.

You're not wrong: if you know how much memory you need for a single query and can keep the data in attached SSD (so ephemeral SSD on AWS), scaling vertically will give you the fastest execution time.

However horizontal scaling has advantages in that it's easier to scale up and down incrementally. It gives you more aggregate network bandwidth for accessing disaggregated data. Disaggregation allows for independent scaling of compute and storage. Losing a single machine has a marginal impact on the cluster, which can enable you to use cheaper spot resources.

Basically, it's often easier to operate a system designed around horizontal scaling if you need resiliency.

d1sxeyes · Nov 7, 2026

The problem is that “faster” and “slower” compare speed, which is x units per y time. But here, we’re only comparing time. The semi-legit interpretation is “if one unit takes 22.2ms, how many units can I complete in 35.6ms”, and actually the answer to that is indeed the 1.6 number they mention.

It’s not sensationalist, it’s just a bit sloppy with the word “faster”.

Sesse__ · Nov 7, 2026

It's 60% faster (0.6x faster, 1.6x as fast). Throughput (“how much stuff you can do per unit of time”) is the only reasonable way to describe performance[1], otherwise large speedups are basically impossible to describe in an intuitive way. (If something that took 10s now takes 1s, that's “ten times as fast”, not “zero point nine times faster”.)

[1] Even latency changes are best described in terms of throughput.

malisper · Nov 7, 2026

The query is:

  SELECT item_id, COUNT(*) AS c
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY item_id
  ORDER BY c DESC
  LIMIT 10;
They are getting the top 10 most frequent values of item_id. It's possible for one item_id to be the 11th most popular item across every partition and not the 10th. Then when you sum the counts across all partitions, it becomes the 10th most common.
